title: Does medical debt affect getting a mortgage in 2026?
summary: A federal ban on medical debt reporting was struck down in 2026. Here's what still counts against your credit score and mortgage approval -- and what doesn't.
body_markdown:
Medical debt can still affect your mortgage in 2026, but less than it used to, and the effect depends on which credit scoring model your lender uses.


A federal rule that would have banned medical debt from credit reports was struck down by a federal court, but the three major credit bureaus have voluntarily softened the effect of medical debt on credit.


Plus, some states have enacted their own limits on medical debt reporting.


So, whether you can buy a new home with medical debt on your record depends on your unique borrowing profile and your location.


A pre-approval from a lender is often a fast way to see where you stand.

## What actually changed with medical debt and credit reports in 2026


The headline you may have seen — "medical debt banned from credit reports" — isn't entirely accurate.


In January 2025, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau finalized a rule that would have removed all medical debt from credit reports. A federal court struck it down before it took effect, and as of 2026 it has no legal force.


What actually happened is smaller, but still meaningful. The three nationwide bureaus — Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion — voluntarily adopted their own policies: paid medical collections are removed entirely, and unpaid collections under $500 no longer appear at all.


That's real relief, but it leaves a gap. An unpaid collection over $500 can still show up. And a voluntary bureau policy isn't a legal guarantee.


## Which credit score model actually matters for your mortgage


Even when a medical collection does appear, whether it hurts your score depends entirely on which scoring model your lender uses which is the lender's choice, not yours.


Older and more common: **FICO 8** is still the most widely used model in mortgage lending. It counts unpaid medical collections over $500 like most other collections, and a single one can pull a 720 score into the 630–670 range.


Newer, less universal: **FICO 9, FICO 10, and VantageScore 4.0** all exclude medical collections from the score, paid or unpaid. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have approved lenders to use VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T as alternatives to Classic FICO, but adoption is staged — not every lender has switched, and FHA's own timeline is separate and still pending.


The practical result: two borrowers with an identical $2,000 unpaid medical collection could see very different outcomes depending on which lender and model evaluates their file.

## Does your state offer extra protection?


With no federal ban, at least 15 states have passed their own medical debt reporting laws as of early 2026, including California, Colorado, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Minnesota, Nevada, New York, and Washington.


Specifics vary: some ban medical debt reporting outright, others raise the threshold above $500 or extend waiting periods, and a few prohibit medical debt from factoring into mortgage decisions specifically.


These protections are also legally contested. The CFPB issued an interpretive rule in late 2025 arguing federal law preempts them, and industry groups have sued to overturn state laws, starting with Colorado. Whether your state's protection holds up is still being litigated.


### How to find out what's actually on your report right now


Before you assume either the best or the worst case, check directly:


- **Pull all three credit reports** (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) — they don't always match.
- **Identify each medical collection's status** : paid or unpaid, dollar amount, and age.
- **Check for errors.** Duplicate accounts, wrong balances, or debts that aren't yours are common with medical billing.
- **Dispute anything inaccurate** directly with the bureau before you apply — disputes can take 30 days or more to resolve.


If other debt might be dragging your score down alongside a medical collection,[this breakdown of what debt to pay off first](https://better.com/content/what-debt-should-i-pay-off-first-to-raise-my-credit-score) can help you prioritize.


## What to do if a medical collection is affecting your mortgage application


If you've checked your reports and a medical collection is still showing up and still counting against your score, a few paths are worth considering:


- **Ask your loan officer which scoring model applies to your application.** This is the single most useful question you can ask. It tells you whether the collection is even being counted.
- **Pay it off if you can.** All three bureaus remove paid medical collections regardless of scoring model, so paying it down helps even under FICO 8.
- **Negotiate directly with the collector or provider.** Many will accept a reduced lump-sum payment, especially for older debts, and some agree to a "pay for delete" arrangement in writing before you pay.
- **Lean on the rest of your file.** A lower score from a medical collection doesn't disqualify you if your[debt-to-income ratio](https://better.com/content/improving-your-debt-to-income-ratio-dti-when-applying-for-a-mortgage) is strong and your income documentation and reserves are solid. Gather your[pre-approval documents](https://better.com/content/documents-needed-for-mortgage-pre-approval) early so a lender sees your full picture, not just one number.
- **Consider a government-backed loan if you qualify.** FHA and VA loans generally allow more flexibility around credit history than conventional loans;[VA loan credit score requirements](https://better.com/content/credit-score-for-va-loan) are typically more forgiving.


None of these fixes happen overnight, but knowing which lever actually moves your situation saves time and money.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### I have an old medical bill in collections. Will that stop me from getting a mortgage?


Not automatically. It depends on whether it's paid, how large it is, and which scoring model your lender uses. A collection under $500 shouldn't appear on your report at all, and a paid collection of any size is supposed to be removed. An unpaid collection over $500 can still count under FICO 8, but it's one factor among many, not an automatic denial.


### My medical collection is $300. Does that even show up on my credit report anymore?


It shouldn't. All three major bureaus have voluntarily stopped reporting medical collections under $500, paid or unpaid. Pull your reports to confirm it's actually been removed, since errors do happen.


### Is there really a law that removed medical debt from credit reports in 2026?


No. The CFPB finalized a rule to do that in January 2025, but a federal court struck it down before it took effect, so there's currently no federal ban. What exists instead is a mix of voluntary bureau policies and state laws, which vary and are still being challenged in court in some cases.


### I paid off my medical collection last year. Why is my score still lower than I expected?


If the payoff was recent, it can take time for bureaus to process the update. It's also possible other factors, such as new inquiries, other collections, or overall credit utilization, are affecting your score independently. Pull your current reports to confirm the paid collection was actually removed.


### Does it matter if my medical debt is old versus something that just went to collections?


Yes, in a few ways. Older debts are more likely to have billing or reporting errors worth disputing, and some state laws extend waiting periods before newer medical debt can be reported at all. Regardless of age, a paid collection should be removed, and any collection under $500 shouldn't appear.


### Is a $15,000 medical collection from a surgery treated differently than a $15,000 credit card balance by my mortgage lender?


For scoring, it depends a lot on the model: FICO 9, FICO 10, and VantageScore 4.0 treat medical collections more leniently than other collections, while FICO 8 generally doesn't distinguish between medical and non-medical collections.


For debt-to-income purposes, a paid-off medical collection doesn't count as ongoing monthly debt the way a credit card balance does.


### I live in a state that passed a medical debt law. Am I fully protected when I apply for a mortgage?


Not necessarily. State protections vary in scope, and several are currently being challenged in court on federal preemption grounds. Treat a state law as meaningful but not guaranteed, and verify directly with your lender how a specific collection is being treated.


### How do I find out which credit scoring model my mortgage lender is actually using?


Ask directly. Lenders aren't required to volunteer this upfront, but loan officers can tell you which model generated your application score, and some can pull an additional model if the first one doesn't reflect your creditworthiness fairly.


## The bottom line


Medical debt in 2026 is genuinely messier than the headlines suggest: no federal ban, a patchwork of state protections under legal challenge, and outcomes that depend heavily on which scoring model your lender uses.


The good news is this is one of the more actionable credit situations you can face. Paid collections and small balances are already supposed to be gone, and the rest comes down to specific, checkable facts about your report and your lender's process.
